voyage.title: Vasco da Gama and the Sea Road to India (1497-1499)
voyage.ships: São Gabriel, São Rafael, Berrio and a storeship
voyage.sponsor: sailing from Lisbon for King Manuel I of Portugal
voyage.summary: The voyage that joined Europe to the Indian Ocean: a long arc into the open Atlantic to catch the westerlies, the Cape rounded ten years after Dias, up the Swahili coast past Mozambique and Mombasa to Malindi, and across to Calicut with a pilot who knew the monsoon.
voyage.what_was_lost: The Roteiro was kept during the voyage by someone aboard — and nobody knows who. It is signed by no one; Álvaro Velho is a guess. Da Gama's own report to the king is lost. Of roughly 170 men who sailed, some 55 came back, and the journal breaks off before the end.

waypoints.event: Vasco da Gama and his fleet departed from Lisbon, beginning their historic voyage to India under the command of King Dom Manuel.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: We left Restello[28] on Saturday, July 8, 1497. May God our Lord permit us to accomplish this voyage in his service. Amen!
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)

waypoints.event: Vasco da Gama's fleet arrived and lay at anchor in the harbour of São Thiago, the largest of the Cape Verde Islands, after a voyage of about fourteen days from Lisbon.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: reached the Ilha do Sal, 1,590 miles from Lisbon, in the course of fourteen days, if not earlier, and on July 27th the little armada lay snugly in the harbour of São Thiago.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)

waypoints.place_modern: Gulf of Guinea, Atlantic Ocean (off West Africa)
waypoints.event: Vasco da Gama's fleet, after leaving São Thiago, sailed in the direction of the Guinea coast and encountered the doldrums, with calms, baffling winds, and squalls, before eventually crossing the equator.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: His actual course, in any case, must have been a circuitous one, and we may suppose it to have been as follows:—Having left São Thiago in an easterly direction,[431] he kept in the direction of the coast for a considerable distance, but when he came within the influence of the dreaded _doldrums_ he met with unpleasant weather in the shape of calms, baffling winds, and squalls, which prevail more especially during the months of June, July, and August.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)

waypoints.place_modern: St. Helena Bay, Western Cape, South Africa
waypoints.event: Vasco da Gama's fleet returned to the land and entered a broad bay, which they named Santa Helena. They sent a boat to take soundings, found good anchorage, and anchored there, remaining for eight days to clean and repair the ships and take on wood.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: On Tuesday [November 7] we returned to the land, which we found to be low, with a broad bay opening into it. The captain-major sent Pero d’Alenquer[43] in a boat to take soundings and to search for good anchoring ground. The bay was found to be very clean, and to afford shelter against all winds except those from the N.W. It extended east and west, and we named it Santa Helena.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)

waypoints.place_modern: Mossel Bay, Western Cape, South Africa
waypoints.event: Vasco da Gama's fleet entered the bay of Sam Brás (now Mossel Bay), where they remained for thirteen days, broke up their store-ship, and transferred its contents to the other vessels.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: Late on Saturday, November 25, the day of St. Catherine’s, we entered the bay (angra) of Sam Brás, where we remained for thirteen days, for there we broke up our store-ship and transferred her contents to the other vessels.[56]
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)

waypoints.place_modern: Cape of Good Hope, South Africa
waypoints.event: Vasco da Gama and his fleet succeeded in doubling the Cape of Good Hope after several days of adverse winds, finally rounding the Cape on November 22, 1497, and then continued along the coast.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: At last, on Wednesday [November 22], at noon, having the wind astern, we succeeded in doubling the Cape, and then ran along the coast.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)

waypoints.place_modern: Great Fish River, Eastern Cape, South Africa

waypoints.event: On Christmas Day, Vasco da Gama's fleet reached the coast of Natal, having discovered seventy leagues of new coastline beyond Dias’ furthest point. The crew discovered that the mast had sprung and made temporary repairs, hoping to fix it properly in a sheltered port.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: By Christmas Day, the 25th of December, we had discovered seventy leagues of coast [beyond Dias’ furthest]. On that day, after dinner, when setting a bonnet, we discovered that the mast had sprung ... and ... secured it with lashings below the top, and that the crack opened and shut. We patched it up with backstays, hoping to be able to repair it thoroughly as soon as we should reach a sheltered port.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)

waypoints.event: Vasco da Gama's fleet arrived off Mozambique Island on March 2, 1498, anchoring in front of the town after following the coast for six days.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: On February 24th the vessels once more gained the open sea, and following the coast for six days arrived off Mozambique on March 2nd. During this voyage of 330 miles they kept outside the islands which here skirt the coast, and lay to at night, as usual, which accounts for the slow rate of progress made during this coasting voyage. Coelho, as before, led the way, and entered by the shallow southern channel, between the islands of S. Thiago and S. Jorge. The three vessels anchored in front of the town (see p. 23).
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)

waypoints.event: The Portuguese fleet anchored off Mombaça (Mombasa) on April 7, 1498, but did not enter the port. They were met by local vessels, exchanged displays of flags, and hoped to go ashore to meet Christians reportedly living there, but were instead met with suspicion and an attempted boarding by armed men.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: On Saturday [April 7] we cast anchor off Mombaça, but did not enter the port. No sooner had we been perceived than a _zavra_[113] manned by Moors came out to us: in front of the city there lay numerous vessels all dressed in flags.[114] And we, anxious not to be outdone, also dressed our ships, and we actually surpassed their show, for we wanted in nothing but men, even the few whom we had being very ill.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)

waypoints.event: Vasco da Gama's fleet anchored off Malindi on April 14, 1498, where they were warmly received and remained for nine days, enjoying festivities and securing a pilot for the crossing to India.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: That same day [April 14] at sunset, we cast anchor off a place called Milinde (Malindi),[121] which is thirty leagues from Mombaça. The following places are between Mombaça and Milinde, viz., Benapa, Toça and Nuguoquioniete.[122]
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)

waypoints.event: On April 24th, Vasco da Gama and his fleet departed from Melinde, having secured a Gujarati pilot, and began their crossing of the Arabian Sea toward India, aided by the southwest monsoon.
waypoints.diary_excerpt:
On April 24th Vasco da Gama, who had secured the services of a Gujarati
pilot, started for India. By that time the S.W. monsoon was blowing
steadily, though not as yet very strongly. The African coast was kept
in sight for a couple of days, after which the vessels stood boldly
across the “Great Gulf.”
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)

waypoints.event: Vasco da Gama and his fleet arrived off the coast of Calecut (modern Kozhikode), sighting the land on May 18th, 1498, and soon after took up a position in front of the city, marking the first direct European sea voyage to India.
waypoints.diary_excerpt:
On April 24th Vasco da Gama, who had secured the services of a Gujarati
pilot, started for India. By that time the S.W. monsoon was blowing
steadily, though not as yet very strongly. The African coast was kept
in sight for a couple of days, after which the vessels stood boldly
across the “Great Gulf.” They passed in all probability to the south of
the _Baixos de Padua_. They had been twenty-one days at sea, and were
still 24 miles from the land, when there rose in front of them a lofty
wooded mountain. This was Mount Eli, 2,220 miles from Melinde, and the
day on which India was first beheld by Europeans who had come direct
from a European port was May 18th, a Friday (see p. 47).[447]
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)

waypoints.event: Vasco da Gama's fleet arrived off the coast of Calecut (Calicut), anchoring two leagues from the city after mistaking the nearby town of Capua for their destination. Local boats approached, and the Portuguese learned they were indeed in sight of Calecut.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: That night [May 20] we anchored two leagues from the city of Calecut, and we did so because our pilot mistook _Capua_,[142] a town at that place, for Calecut. Still further[143] there is another town called _Pandarani_.[144] We anchored about a league and a half from the shore. After we were at anchor, four boats (_almadias_) approached us from the land, who asked of what nation we were. We told them, and they then pointed out Calecut to us.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)

waypoints.event: Vasco da Gama arrived at the Anjediva Islands, where he landed on the largest island and remained until October 5th, careening his ships and waiting for favorable winds for the return voyage.
waypoints.diary_excerpt:
On September 20th Vasco da Gama arrived at the Anjediva Islands, about
14° 45´ N., having thus spent twenty-one days in accomplishing 240
miles. He seems, first of all, to have anchored near the Oyster Rocks,
off the Kalipadi river, but on September 24th he landed on the largest
of these islands, where he remained until October 5th, waiting for a
propitious wind, and availed himself of the enforced leisure to careen
the flagship and the _Berrio_ (p. 83).
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)

waypoints.event: Vasco da Gama's fleet anchored off Malindi on the return voyage, where they sought pilots and provisions, and remained for several days while interacting with the local inhabitants.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: That same day [April 14] at sunset, we cast anchor off a place called Milinde (Malindi),[121] which is thirty leagues from Mombaça.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)

waypoints.event: Vasco da Gama's fleet arrived off Mozambique Island on March 2nd, 1499, anchoring in front of the town after following the coast for six days. They later moved to the island of S. Jorge, where mass was read before continuing their voyage north.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: On February 24th the vessels once more gained the open sea, and following the coast for six days arrived off Mozambique on March 2nd. During this voyage of 330 miles they kept outside the islands which here skirt the coast, and lay to at night, as usual, which accounts for the slow rate of progress made during this coasting voyage. Coelho, as before, led the way, and entered by the shallow southern channel, between the islands of S. Thiago and S. Jorge. The three vessels anchored in front of the town (see p. 23). Later on they removed to the island of S. Jorge, where mass was read on March 12th, after which the little flotilla set sail for the north.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)

waypoints.place_modern: Cape of Good Hope, South Africa
waypoints.event: Vasco da Gama and his fleet succeeded in rounding the Cape of Good Hope after several days of adverse winds, finally doubling the Cape on November 22, 1497, and then continued along the coast.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: At last, on Wednesday [November 22], at noon, having the wind astern, we succeeded in doubling the Cape, and then ran along the coast.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)

waypoints.place_modern: Angra do Heroísmo, Terceira Island, Azores, Portugal
waypoints.event: Vasco da Gama brought his dying brother Paulo da Gama to the Angra of Terceira, where Paulo died a day after landing and was buried in the church of the Monastery of S. Francisco.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: Paulo died a day after he had landed at the Angra of Terceira, and was buried in the church of the Monastery of S. Francisco.[236] A resident of Terceira, one Arthur Rodriguez, at once started in a caravel to carry the news of Vasco da Gama’s arrival to Lisbon.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)

waypoints.event: Vasco da Gama returned to Lisbon after his first voyage to India, arriving in a caravel on August 29th, 1499, following the death and burial of his brother Paulo da Gama on Terceira.
waypoints.diary_excerpt:
Vasco da Gama himself reached Lisbon in a caravel on August
29th, two years and nearly two months after he had left that
port.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 (trans. E. G. Ravenstein, Hakluyt Society, 1898)
